eyebrow: Azure & AWS Cloud Security Engineering · Chapter 6
titlePlain: Encryption at Rest and in Transit:
subtitle: Lesson 21 · Data Protection in the Cloud

steps.label: Platform-managed (default)
steps.sub: Microsoft/AWS generates, stores, and rotates the key — free, sufficient for most workloads

steps.label: Customer-managed key (CMK)
steps.sub: you own the key in Key Vault/KMS; you can revoke it on demand

steps.label: The real difference is control
steps.sub: not encryption strength — both models encrypt the same way

eyebrow: Where CMK plugs in, per service
code:
# Azure
#  Storage (blobs)  -> Storage Service Encryption, swap to CMK via Key Vault
#  Azure SQL        -> TDE, bring your own TDE protector key
#  Azure Disk Encryption -> BitLocker/dm-crypt, CMK by design

# AWS
#  S3   -> SSE-S3 (AWS key) | SSE-KMS (AWS or customer KMS key) | SSE-C (you supply it)
#  EBS  -> encrypted by default, backed by a KMS key
#  RDS  -> set at creation, backed by a KMS key
caption: Same pattern on both clouds: a key vault service sits behind the data service.

eyebrow: Encryption in transit is enforced, not assumed
caption: At-rest encryption being on by default does not mean in-transit is enforced — check both.

eyebrow: When CMK is worth the overhead

steps.label: Compliance or contract requires independent revocation
steps.sub: you must be able to cut off access without the provider's involvement

steps.label: You need a key-level audit trail
steps.sub: Key Vault and KMS log every single key operation

steps.label: Otherwise, platform-managed is not a lesser posture
steps.sub: same encryption, managed by a dedicated key-management team
